newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Hun Sen warns big powers not to meddle.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Hun Sen warns big powers not to meddle.

text.p: Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen said on Monday he might drop Cambodia's bid to join the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) and warned big powers not to use aid as a weapon to pressure him.

Hun Sen's strident rejection of outside interference in Cambodia's internal affairs came as King Norodom Sihanouk said he doubted that efforts by foreign envoys to negotiate an end to Cambodia's crisis would succeed.
"We consider if we go to ASEAN or if we stop. I want to stop if ASEAN continues to interfere in our internal affairs," Hun Sen told reporters in Kompong Thom province, north of the capital.

The seven-member group last week postponed Cambodia's membership indefinitely in response to Hun Sen's ouster of First Prime Minster Prince Norodom Ranariddh on July 6 after two days of fighting in Phnom Penh.
"I am afraid of joining ASEAN because of ASEAN interference in internal affairs," he said. He said he was discussing the matter with his senior ministers.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. Cambodia had been due to join this month along with Laos and Burma.
ASEAN said last week it still recognised Ranariddh as first prime minister and would try to work out a ceasefire between forces loyal to the rival premiers.
Hun Sen also warned Cambodia's aid donors not to try to pressure him with threats of aid cuts.
"You cannot come and say 'Excellency, you must do this or do that because my country has helped you a lot'," Hun Sen said of aid donors.
"Business is different from aid. You should not want to threaten Hun Sen, you can threaten anyone else, that's all right, but not Hun Sen," he said.
The United States last week suspended aid to Cambodia for 30 days in response to Ranariddh's overthrow. Germany suspended aid indefinitely and Australia said it was considering suspending aid.
Cambodia gets half its annual budget from overseas donations.

King Sihanouk said on Monday he was doubtful efforts by ASEAN, as well as by France, the United States and Japan to push for a negotiated settlement to Cambodia's crisis, would succeed in the light of Hun Sen's rejection of an earlier offer to hold reconciliation talks.
The king, who is in Beijing for medical treatment, said he was willing to meet envoys from ASEAN and the three countries who he said were due in Beijing this week.

Sihanouk and the envoys were "not authorised by 'The Strongman' (Hun Sen) to intervene in that which is called the internal affairs of Cambodia", the king said in an interview with his information bulletin, released by the palace on Monday.
"Hun Sen has already clearly rejected my proposals of mediation," the king said.
Sihanouk called on his son, Ranariddh, and Hun Sen to meet him in Beijing for mediation talks after their forces began fighting in the capital on July 5.
The next day, as Hun Sen's troops were pushing Ranariddh's men out of the Phnom Penh, Hun Sen announced Ranariddh's ouster and said bluntly there was no need for the king's mediation talks.
Sihanouk indicated on Sunday that he would not endorse Cambodia's new government, but stopped short of accusing Hun Sen of staging a coup.
Foreign Minister Ung Huot, a member of Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party, returned to Cambodia on Monday saying he wanted to work for democracy and pluralism.
Many FUNCINPEC members and sympathisers fled from the country in the aftermath of Ranariddh's ouster and the execution of Ho Sok, a FUNCINPEC secretary of state at the interior ministry.
Hun Sen confirmed on Monday that Chao Sambath, a FUNCINPEC intelligence officer, had also been killed in the recent fighting.
Opposition leader Sam Rainsy, an ally of Ranariddh, was due to return to Cambodia overland from Thailand on Monday, opposition and Thai army sources said.
